name: Beacon
tagline: A Databricks lakehouse that traces how financial markets respond to macroeconomic conditions.
problem: Macro releases move markets, but the relationship is scattered across a dozen data providers and rarely queryable in one place. You either read a Fed report or a stock chart, not both at once.
built: An end-to-end lakehouse on a medallion architecture: batch and streaming ingestion in PySpark from FRED macroeconomic series and market data (Tiingo, Finnhub), transformation in dbt-databricks, and orchestration as a single daily Databricks Workflows DAG defined in an asset bundle. Two Claude-powered agents keep it healthy: one diagnoses data quality failures after every ingest, the other reviews every change pushed to the repo.

agents.name: Data quality agent
agents.summary: After every daily ingest, about a dozen rule-based checks (freshness, duplicate keys, OHLC sanity, per-series FRED lag, job-run health) write their results to an ops table. Only when something fails, a Claude agent investigates the failures and writes a root-cause report.
points: Investigates with read-only tools: SQL against the lakehouse, Databricks job-run history with error traces, and the project’s own source code.
Separates real data problems from thresholds that are too strict, like a market holiday or a FRED release delay, and checks whether a failure is new or ongoing.
Guardrails: a single-statement SQL allowlist plus a write-keyword denylist, file reads confined to project folders, API-key scrubbing, a 15-turn cap, and token counts logged per incident.
Runs in the daily DAG even when ingest fails (run_if: ALL_DONE); an error-severity failure fails the job and emails a link to the diagnosis.

agents.name: AI code review
agents.summary: Every push to master is reviewed by Claude (the Claude Code GitHub Action) against a Beacon-specific checklist: MERGE idempotency, watermark edge cases, secrets handling, and Databricks Free Edition concurrency limits. Major or blocker findings open a GitHub issue.
points: Works around the action not accepting push events with a two-hop workflow: the push re-dispatches the review through workflow_dispatch with the pushed commit range.
Specced a custom reviewer as the next step: static checks first, structured JSON findings, and an eval set of seeded bugs drawn from the project’s own history.

architecture: Bronze — raw FRED and market data, batch and Structured Streaming ingest via PySpark
Silver — cleaned, conformed series in Delta Lake
Gold — dbt-databricks models joining macro and market signals
Serve — next: an MCP server exposing the gold layer to a natural-language analytics agent
Quality — rule-based checks after every ingest; a Claude agent diagnoses anything that fails
outcome: In progress — the medallion pipeline, gold-layer models, and the data quality agent run as one daily DAG, and AI code review runs on every push. Next milestone: the MCP server for the analytics agent.

name: SQL Server Deployment Automation
tagline: SQL Server deployment automation that cut configuration time by 90% and cut project time by three months

context.source: Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

problem: We had six months to replace hundreds of SQL Server instances. Configuring each manually took hours.
built: I built PowerShell and T-SQL scripts that saved me (and my boss) 6+ hours daily. I turn it from manually selecting options in Server Manager to clicking two buttons for each server and turning a 2+ hour process into less than 15 minutes.

comparison.label: before
comparison.note: Manual Server Manager setup: 2+ hours per server

name: Data Science Distribution Forecasting
tagline: A production-deployed forecasting service for a regional distribution center.
problem: A regional distribution center needed a repeatable, automated forecast of weekly demand instead of a spreadsheet re-run by hand — and needed it accurate enough to plan against.
built: Weekly demand forecasting in R with modeltime and tidymodels. I tested dozens of models and fine-tuned what I got to get the best outcomes for seasonal demand. The selected model was Prophet on a log-transformed target with exogenous regressors: a peak-period flag, average temperature, and a transport cost index.
architecture: Weekly demand data → feature engineering in R (modeltime / tidymodels)
Prophet on a log-transformed target with exogenous regressors
Model pinned to an S3 board via vetiver
Served as a containerized API via plumber
outcome: Cut MAE roughly 26% against a normal-scale Prophet baseline.

featuredMetric.label: lower forecast error (MAE) vs. a baseline Prophet model

comparison.label: baseline
comparison.note: Normal-scale Prophet baseline, MAE indexed to 100

comparison.label: final
comparison.note: Log-target Prophet with regressors: ~26% lower MAE

name: Production Data Monitoring
tagline: Making sure critical banking data doesn't disappear
problem: Data warehouse data at Zions is complex and there is so much that, if some goes missing, it is hard to know that it did and where it went.
built: I built a data pipeline with 50+ unique tests to verify that no critical data goes missing and makes sure it stays inside of statistical boundaries.

featuredMetric.label: automated tests guarding critical banking data

name: QueryCraft
tagline: A visual SQL learning environment for students who don't write SQL yet.
problem: I tutored far too many students in SQL and watched them struggle to understand the basics. This is an easy way to get in there and visually learn how SQL works and complete tasks that build your skills.
built: A drag-and-drop query builder, a dropdown builder, a full SQL IDE, an ERD canvas, and a chart visualizer, all over a metadata-provider architecture that supports PostgreSQL and MySQL. Built spec-first from a written PRD, with Kano analysis behind the feature set. The UI uses dnd-kit and a Ctrl+K command palette.
outcome: Approaching MVP — the core builder, IDE, ERD canvas, and visualizer are functional; current work is closing gaps against the Kano-prioritized feature set.

name: Life Dashboard
tagline: A private, one-screen dashboard for my day, with a Claude assistant that can act on my email and calendar.
problem: My day was spread across Canvas, Gmail, Google Calendar, bank exports, the weather and a hiking app. Checking all of them every morning took longer than the things they were telling me to do.
built: A FastAPI app with a plain HTML/CSS/JS front end and SQLite that fits on one screen without scrolling. It pulls Canvas assignments, Gmail and Google Calendar (read-only, multiple accounts), card spending from CSV exports, nearby trails from OpenStreetMap with a 7-day forecast, and a national park photo of the day. The calendar has week, month and hour views with color-coding, and a morning brief sums up the day in one card. Every 15 minutes a background job scans new email for to-dos and events.

agents.name: Dashboard assistant
agents.summary: Ask in plain English ("find my interview emails and remind me to send thank-yous on Friday") and a Claude tool loop searches and reads email, checks the calendar and to-do list, then adds to-dos or suggests events.
points: A deliberately narrow tool set: read-only email search and read, calendar list, to-do list, create a to-do, suggest an event. Nothing can send or delete email or write to Google directly.
Suggested events wait for my approval before anything reaches Google Calendar, and a deterministic event ID means approving twice can't create a duplicate.
Runs in a background thread with live progress, one run at a time, a daily cap and a turn limit; long digit runs are masked before any text reaches the model.

agents.name: Inbox triage
agents.summary: New mail goes through fixed rules first (a grocery delivery lands on the calendar), then a small Claude model returns schema-validated JSON deciding whether a message is a to-do, an event to suggest, or nothing.
points: Caching and daily caps keep the cost predictable; replies are validated and only ever shown as plain text.

architecture: Sources — Canvas, Gmail, Google Calendar, card CSVs, OpenStreetMap trails, NWS weather, NPS photos
App — FastAPI and SQLite on a small AWS EC2 instance, with systemd timers for the 15-minute jobs
Access — Cloudflare Tunnel (no open ports) and Cloudflare Access, with the login token verified again inside the app
AI — Claude for inbox triage and the tool-using assistant; calendar writes need my approval
Ops — nightly SQLite backups with integrity checks, and 189 automated tests
outcome: Live and in daily use on my laptop and phone.

name: Turtle Shelter Project Website
tagline: Competed to build the best solution for a nonprofit that was looking to scale their humanitarian reach.
problem: A local humanitarian nonprofit was running everything with a generic website and a database that consisted of a memo on an iPhone.
built: On a team of four I worked as the cloud solution architect and database engineer to build a web application that hosted real-time data for a nonprofit. I made sure that data would report instantly from the cloud database to the dashboard and other metrics tracking devices on the site.

name: lavender.
tagline: A family of data tools for people who live in warehouses: lineage, masking, cost, data quality and SQL learning under one sign-in.
problem: Warehouse teams juggle separate tools for lineage, PII masking, cost and data quality, each with its own login, connections and look. I wanted to see how far one person could get designing them as a single, consistent suite.
built: A suite of products on one design system and one shared connector layer (Databricks, Snowflake, SQL Server, Oracle, Postgres, DuckDB): dataview maps the whole warehouse with column-level lineage and pull-request impact; masking produces consistent, referentially intact masked data for dev and test; ledger splits the warehouse bill along the lineage graph per table, owner and pull request; pulse flags columns that leave their normal range, drift or go stale; QueryCraft teaches SQL visually; and datasuite ties them together with one sign-in, shared encrypted connections and suite-wide search.

agents.name: Overnight Claude Code runs
agents.summary: Much of the suite was built in unattended Claude Code sessions working from a written brief I authored: ground rules, the order of work, and the bar for calling something done. My feedback batches steered each next round.
points: Guardrails in the brief: stay inside the repo, commit after every finished unit of work, never push or rewrite history, no real credentials or warehouses, and tests must pass before anything counts as done.
Two runs a night coordinated through a status file and a running log that ends in a hand-off for the next session.

outcome: Prototypes and MVPs running on demo data, with CI linting and testing every product on each push; dataview has also been run against a real Databricks workspace.
